analysis.investment_thesis: Arvind is a classic slow-grower — revenue of ₹8,329 Cr in 2025 barely exceeds ₹9,221 Cr in 2017, with a 9-year revenue CAGR of just 0.4%. At 24x earnings with no credible growth engine, this is an expensive ticket for a stalled business.
key_strengths: Debt deleveraging has been impressive — borrowings nearly halved from ₹2,640 Cr (2020) to ₹1,448 Cr (2024), keeping D/E at a manageable 0.39
Operating cash flow consistently positive across all 5 years (₹596–763 Cr range), showing the core textile business isn't a cash sink
Gross margin of 49% signals brand/product mix quality above commodity textile peers
key_risks: Zero real revenue growth over 9 years — ₹8,011 Cr in 2016 to ₹8,329 Cr in 2025 is essentially inflation-adjusted decline
Classic 'diworsification' — sprawling into e-commerce, agriculture, telecom, real estate, and water treatment destroys focus with no visible payoff
Capex spiked to ₹535 Cr in FY25 (vs ₹278 Cr prior year), crushing FCF to ₹280 Cr; CWIP jumped to ₹331 Cr — capital deployment risk without proven ROI
red_flags: PEG ratio is disastrous: P/E of 24x against realistic earnings growth of ~4% (FY24→FY25: ₹353→₹367 Cr) implies PEG of ~6x — far above Lynch's 1.0 ceiling
ROE of 9.3% is below Lynch's 12% minimum threshold — the business earns less than it should on equity
Revenue in FY25 (₹8,329 Cr) still cannot clear FY17 revenue (₹9,221 Cr) after nearly a decade — the story is not progressing
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Arvind is what I'd call a "slow grower in denial" — a 127-year-old textile manufacturer trying to dress itself up as a diversified industrial play. The numbers don't lie: a 0.4% revenue CAGR over 9 years and a -3.1% EBITDA CAGR in the same period mean the company has been running to stand still while India's economy compounded at 6-7% annually. The recent 5-year "expanding" trend is nothing more than COVID-base recovery — revenue in FY25 still can't beat FY17 levels. At ₹387, you're paying 24x trailing earnings for this privilege.

The balance sheet has genuinely improved — debt reduction from ₹2,640 Cr to ₹1,537 Cr over five years is real and commendable. But the FY25 capex surge to ₹535 Cr raises a concern: is this a genuine capacity investment for growth (advanced materials, technical textiles), or empire-building in a business that has historically not earned its cost of capital? With ROE at 9.3%, the answer leans toward the latter. The sprawl into water treatment, telecom, real estate, and agriculture is textbook "diworsification" — the exact trap I warn investors about. For a ten-bagger, I need a simple story I can explain in two minutes. Arvind needs a whiteboard and a flowchart.
